# Product-Adaptation Strategy for a Voice Assistant Entering Honorific-Language Markets (2026)

## Executive Recommendation

Honorific systems are not features; they are architectures. A voice assistant entering Japan, Korea, Thailand, and the Gulf cannot treat politeness, household structure, and privacy as localization layers to bolt on top of a Western design. The Western voice assistant was built on three assumptions that each of these markets violates structurally:

1. **One user, one relationship** — Western assistants assume a single primary user with a casual, often first-name relationship. Honorific-language markets operate on multi-user, role-defined relationships where the device's stance toward each speaker is structurally different.

2. **Privacy as transactional consent** — Western models treat privacy as a one-time install consent plus a privacy policy. These markets treat privacy as a continuous, household-level, culturally embedded concern tied to who is in the room and what is being said in front of whom.

3. **Initiative belongs to the user** — Western assistants are designed to be proactive (suggestions, reminders, ambient awareness). Honorific cultures assign initiative asymmetries between speakers; an assistant that volunteers too freely can read as presumptuous, intrusive, or disrespectful.

The recommended approach: **rebuild the interaction model around four anchors** — honorifics as core architecture, the household as the unit of design (not the individual), privacy as visible and structural (not just policy), and cultural/religious calendars as first-class features (not edge cases). Ship fewer features done right rather than the full Western feature set done poorly.

The market entry is not four rollouts of the same product. It is **four products with a shared architectural spine**, where the spine (NLP pipeline, voice biometric engine, household orchestration, privacy hardware signals, calendar engine) is common and the visible interaction layer is deeply market-specific.

---

## 1. Why Western Design Assumptions Break — The Mismatch Map

| Western Assumption | Japan | Korea | Thailand | Gulf |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Casual, first-name interaction** | Breaks keigo — assistant must default to teineigo or above | Breaks jondaetmal/banmal split — wrong register reads as rude | Breaks phu-yai/phu-noi hierarchy — too casual reads as disrespect | Breaks khaleeji hospitality norms — wrong formality offends |
| **Single primary user** | Breaks multigenerational household — grandmother's requests must work as well as teenager's | Increasingly nuclear but still significant multigen | Multigenerational households common — grandparent respect is central | Multilingual, multigenerational, often with household staff — multiple "user classes" in one home |
| **Always-listening is acceptable in exchange for utility** | High concern post-APPI scandals; physical mute is a must-have | PIPA-strict; always-on cloud processing of voice is contested | Growing concern with PDPA (2022); cultural preference for less intrusion | Religious/cultural concerns about perpetual surveillance; household staff privacy |
| **Proactive suggestions welcome** | Reads as presumptuous; "kashikomatta" means well-mannered restraint | Mixed — younger users accept, older users don't | Breaks "kreng jai" (reluctance to impose) — proactive suggestions are unwelcome | Breaks hospitality etiquette — assistant should not interrupt or volunteer |
| **English/French/German first, others later** | Japanese-first or nothing — users abandon products that don't understand keigo and dialect | Korean-first or nothing — Samsung Bixby, Kakao, Naver set the bar | Thai-first or nothing — tonal language errors are immediately disqualifying | Arabic-first (MSA + Khaleeji) or nothing — Gulf-specific dialect or it fails |
| **Religious/secular framing** | Secular default is fine; Shinto/Buddhist calendar optional | Secular default fine; some Christian calendar features | Buddhist calendar (Wan Phra) and merit-making context important | Islamic framing essential — prayer, Hijri, Ramadan, Quran awareness |
| **Calendar = Gregorian** | Gregorian + Japanese imperial era + seasonal awareness | Gregorian + Korean lunar holidays | Gregorian + Thai lunar calendar + Buddhist holidays | Hijri primary, Gregorian secondary |
| **Personal assistant = "your buddy"** | Helper, not buddy — relationship is functional, hierarchical | Companion with personality — K-content sensibility | Friendly helper, but deferential to elders | Service — avoid anthropomorphism for some users; servant framing more culturally legible |

The asymmetry: a Japanese user will tolerate an imperfect weather forecast but will not tolerate an assistant that uses casual language to their grandmother. A Gulf user will tolerate limited smart home integration but will not tolerate an assistant that interrupts prayer time. Quality is judged by cultural fit before it is judged by feature completeness.

---

## 2. Pillar One — Interaction Style

### 2.1 Japan: Keigo as Architecture

The Japanese honorific system is the most structurally complex in the candidate set. Three forms (plus casual) require the assistant to maintain multiple registers and switch appropriately:

- **Teineigo** (polite plain) — default for the assistant toward any adult user
- **Sonkeigo** (respectful, used to elevate the other person) — required when addressing elders, formal contexts
- **Kenjougo** (humble, used to lower oneself) — required when referring to the assistant's own actions in formal contexts (e.g., "I have prepared…", "Allow me to…")
- **Casual** — never default; opt-in only, typically for younger users' preferred mode

**Architecture**:
- **Speaker profile → register mapping**: voice biometrics identifies the speaker; the system selects register based on the speaker's profile (age, household role) and the relationship between the speaker and any other household member being addressed in the response.
- **Self-reference**: assistant uses "watashi" (formal) by default, never "ore" or "boku" (casual/masculine).
- **Address form**: surnames + "-san" for adults the system knows about; honorific family terms (okāsan, otōsan, oji-san, obā-san) for relatives; "omae" never.
- **Response morphology**: sentences include "gozaimasu", "desu", "masu" endings; honorific o- prefix on action verbs when referring to the user's actions ("o-shimeri", "o-hanami"). Avoid casual contractions, slang, colloquial contractions (e.g., "ちゃん" suffixes).
- **Hesitation markers**: assistants can use "etto" or "ano" naturally when "thinking"; this reads as humanized, not robotic.
- **Visual feedback**: text output uses formal Japanese; furigana for difficult kanji when the user is identified as elderly or child.
- **Voice tone**: warm but reserved; not robotic, not intimate. Pitch slightly lower for elder profiles (research shows Japanese users prefer lower-pitched assistants for elder interactions).
- **Anthropomorphism level**: moderate. Avoid claiming feelings ("I'm happy to help" — too casual); allow expressions of care through verb choice rather than emotional declaration.
- **Dialect support**: Kansai-ben, Tohoku-ben, Kyushu-ben as opt-in. Default never uses dialect. Detect user dialect from voice profile and offer switch.
- **Family member addressing**: when speaking to or about family members, use appropriate kinship terms with honorifics; never use first names without "-san".

### 2.2 Korea: Jondaetmal Default, Banmal Opt-In

Korean has a four-level speech system (hasipsio, haeyo, haerae, panmal) but in practice the social binary of jondaetmal (polite) versus banmal (casual) is what determines whether the assistant sounds appropriate.

**Architecture**:
- **Default jondaetmal (haeyo-che)** for all adult speakers; the assistant uses "jebal" (please), "-seumnida" endings, "nim" honorifics.
- **Banmal opt-in** for users under 30 who explicitly choose casual mode; the assistant uses "-a"/"-eo" endings, no honorifics.
- **Pronoun and address system**: "je" (humble I) for assistant; user addressed as "nim"-suffixed title by default; family terms with honorifics (eomma, appa, halmeoni — no honorifics needed because kinship terms are inherently respectful).
- **Title recognition**: "seonsaengnim" for teachers, "daeri-nim" for managers, etc. — assistant recognizes and uses these when user profile indicates the relationship.
- **Code-switching**: Korean-English is normal in Korea (Konglish); assistant handles mixed-language queries seamlessly.
- **Romanization**: always render in Hangul in visual feedback; never rely on romanization.
- **Sound symbolism**: assistants can use Bang-song-eo (onomatopoeia) in responses where natural — "ding-dong" for doorbell, etc.
- **K-content personality**: voice can carry warmth and brightness without crossing into casual; K-pop sensibility — polished, pleasant, slightly playful for younger profiles.
- **Aegyo (cuteness) layer**: optional opt-in for younger users — adds diminutive forms and a softer voice; inappropriate for older profiles.

### 2.3 Thailand: Three-Way Formality with Royal and Religious Reservations

Thai politeness operates on multiple axes — phu-yai/phu-noi (senior/junior), formal/casual, royal (raachasap), religious (sasana), and gendered pronouns.

**Architecture**:
- **Default polite register** with "kha"/"khraap" particles based on the assistant's voice profile; particles "na", "ka", "krub", "khun" used appropriately.
- **First-person pronouns** for the assistant: avoid gender-marked pronouns unless voice is gender-marked; "dichan" (neutral formal) or "phom" (formal male) — but choose based on voice profile and household expectation.
- **Royal vocabulary**: must be used with extreme care. The assistant should never use raachasap except in proper contexts (e.g., reading official Thai Royal News). Built-in royal vocabulary library with strict usage rules; legal/cultural review of any content involving monarchy.
- **Religious vocabulary**: Buddhist terms (tham, bun, sila) used appropriately; assistant doesn't claim religious authority but can reference merit, mindfulness, alms-giving contexts respectfully.
- **Tonal ASR**: ASR must be trained on Thai tonal variations across regions; tonal errors immediately disqualify the product in user perception.
- **Dialect support**: Central Thai default; Isan, Northern, Southern dialects as opt-in.
- **Kreng jai calibration**: assistant does not volunteer follow-up suggestions; asks "Will that be all?" rather than "Would you also like…?".
- **Sanuk (enjoyment) layer**: light, tasteful humor acceptable; avoid American-style sarcasm that reads as rude.
- **Visual feedback**: formal Thai script; polite particles in text.

### 2.4 Gulf: Khaleeji Hospitality, Religious Reserve, Multilingual Fluency

The Gulf is not a single market but a set of distinct Arabic dialects (Khaleeji in Saudi, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain, UAE, Oman) overlaid on Modern Standard Arabic for formal contexts, with multilingual households where Arabic, English, Hindi/Urdu, Filipino/Tagalog, and other languages are routinely spoken.

**Architecture**:
- **Language detection**: assistant detects spoken language in real time and responds in the same language; multilingual households get multilingual fluency, not single-language-with-translation.
- **Code-switching**: Arabic-English code-switching is the norm in Gulf homes (Arabizi romanized text is also common); assistant handles mid-sentence switches.
- **Diglossia handling**: MSA for formal queries (Quran, news, official information); Khaleeji for everyday queries. User can opt for MSA default if preferred.
- **Religious framing**: assistant framed as a service ("service," "helper," "facilitator") rather than a companion ("friend," "buddy"). Some Islamic scholars consider anthropomorphizing AI impermissible; the assistant avoids emotional self-claims and uses functional language.
- **Religious formula awareness**: "Bismillah" optional acknowledgment for new actions; "Alhamdulillah," "MashaAllah," "SubhanAllah" used appropriately in response contexts; not used gratuitously.
- **Prayer time awareness**: silent or low-activity mode during prayer times (5x daily); Fajr, Dhuhr, Asr, Maghrib, Isha. Do not interrupt; do not volunteer; queue requests and respond after prayer.
- **Ramadan mode**: changes greeting, content sensitivity (food/alcohol queries), schedule awareness (iftar, suhoor), Quran integration option.
- **Gender considerations**: avoid defaulting to female-coded voice for all users — gender preference may vary; offer multiple voice options including gender-neutral synthetic voices.
- **Voice tone**: warm and respectful, but reserved; hospitality register — assistant as courteous service.
- **Calligraphy aesthetic**: visual feedback uses Arabic calligraphy-style typography where appropriate; right-to-left rendering correctly handled.

---

## 3. Pillar Two — Household Roles

### 3.1 The Household as the User

In all four markets, the household is a more natural unit of design than the individual. The Western "primary user + occasional guests" model needs to be replaced with a **household member model** where each person has a voice profile, a role, and relationship rules to other household members.

**Core capabilities**:
- **Voice biometrics**: each household member's voice profile is registered (with consent). The assistant identifies the speaker in real time and adapts interaction accordingly.
- **Household member registry**: explicit family relationships (grandmother, father, eldest son, household staff) with default behavior rules.
- **Role-appropriate responses**: e.g., when child asks for a snack at 10pm, assistant checks parents' settings; when grandmother asks for weather, assistant responds with extra clarity, slower TTS, and elder-friendly vocabulary.
- **Multi-speaker resolution**: when multiple people speak (e.g., "ask the assistant X" while another says "yes, do it"), assistant clarifies before acting on shared intent.

### 3.2 Market-Specific Household Structures

**Japan — Multigenerational with Seniority Hierarchy**
- Three-generation households (grandparents, parents, children) significant — 20%+ of households include elderly members, and ~5–7% are full three-generation.
- Grandparents' requests get full respect and clarity; sonkeigo register; elder-friendly TTS (slower, clearer).
- Children's requests subject to parental controls configurable per parent.
- "Confirmation culture" — assistant confirms before acting on requests that affect shared household state (heating, locks, lights in shared spaces).
- Family schedule coordination: "When is grandmother's doctor appointment?" — assistant integrates individual calendars with respect to seniority and privacy.
- Seniority in voice arbitration: if parents and children request conflicting actions, parents take precedence by default; configurable.

**Korea — Mixed Multigen and Nuclear with Strong Parental Controls**
- Multigenerational households declining but still significant; increasing nuclear family households with strong parental controls.
- Voice biometrics for each family member; parents have authority over children's queries and devices.
- Elder-friendly mode: slower TTS, clearer prompts, larger visual feedback; triggered by voice profile age detection (optional).
- KakaoTalk integration — assistant sends family messages, reads family chat updates (with consent), coordinates schedules.
- Family-shared lists and reminders with role-based editing.
- Children's content filter with parents' approval workflow.

**Thailand — Multigenerational with Grandparent Reverence**
- Multigenerational households common; grandparents revered (cultural and Buddhist context).
- Grandparent voice profiles get priority clarity, polite language, slower response.
- Family prayer/wellness routines: assistant can be configured to support morning/evening Buddhist practices (chanting timer, alms-giving reminder, merit-making reminder) — with explicit opt-in.
- Children's access with parents' controls; respectful default for any elder voice profile.
- Visual feedback uses formal Thai with proper address forms for known family members.

- **On-device processing**: as much processing as possible happens on-device, not in the cloud. Wake-word detection, common commands, voice biometrics all run locally. Only complex queries that require cloud models are sent.

- **Per-query cloud opt-out**: users can configure the device to never send voice to the cloud, accepting reduced capability in exchange.

- **Voice biometric consent**: voice profile registration requires explicit household-level consent (not just individual); any family member can request deletion of their voice profile.

# Product-Adaptation Strategy for a Voice Assistant Entering Honorific-Language Markets (2026)

## Executive Recommendation

Honorific systems are not features; they are architectures. A voice assistant entering Japan, Korea, Thailand, and the Gulf cannot treat politeness, household structure, and privacy as localization layers to bolt on top of a Western design. The Western voice assistant was built on three assumptions that each of these markets violates structurally:

1. **One user, one relationship** — Western assistants assume a single primary user with a casual, often first-name relationship. Honorific-language markets operate on multi-user, role-defined relationships where the device's stance toward each speaker is structurally different.

2. **Privacy as transactional consent** — Western models treat privacy as a one-time install consent plus a privacy policy. These markets treat privacy as a continuous, household-level, culturally embedded concern tied to who is in the room and what is being said in front of whom.

3. **Initiative belongs to the user** — Western assistants are designed to be proactive (suggestions, reminders, ambient awareness). Honorific cultures assign initiative asymmetries between speakers; an assistant that volunteers too freely can read as presumptuous, intrusive, or disrespectful.

The recommended approach: **rebuild the interaction model around four anchors** — honorifics as core architecture, the household as the unit of design (not the individual), privacy as visible and structural (not just policy), and cultural/religious calendars as first-class features (not edge cases). Ship fewer features done right rather than the full Western feature set done poorly.

The market entry is not four rollouts of the same product. It is **four products with a shared architectural spine**, where the spine (NLP pipeline, voice biometric engine, household orchestration, privacy hardware signals, calendar engine) is common and the visible interaction layer is deeply market-specific.

---

## 1. Why Western Design Assumptions Break — The Mismatch Map

| Western Assumption | Japan | Korea | Thailand | Gulf |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Casual, first-name interaction** | Breaks keigo — assistant must default to teineigo or above | Breaks jondaetmal/banmal split — wrong register reads as rude | Breaks phu-yai/phu-noi hierarchy — too casual reads as disrespect | Breaks khaleeji hospitality norms — wrong formality offends |
| **Single primary user** | Breaks multigenerational household — grandmother's requests must work as well as teenager's | Increasingly nuclear but still significant multigen | Multigenerational households common — grandparent respect is central | Multilingual, multigenerational, often with household staff — multiple "user classes" in one home |
| **Always-listening is acceptable in exchange for utility** | High concern post-APPI scandals; physical mute is a must-have | PIPA-strict; always-on cloud processing of voice is contested | Growing concern with PDPA (2022); cultural preference for less intrusion | Religious/cultural concerns about perpetual surveillance; household staff privacy |
| **Proactive suggestions welcome** | Reads as presumptuous; "kashikomatta" means well-mannered restraint | Mixed — younger users accept, older users don't | Breaks "kreng jai" (reluctance to impose) — proactive suggestions are unwelcome | Breaks hospitality etiquette — assistant should not interrupt or volunteer |
| **English/French/German first, others later** | Japanese-first or nothing — users abandon products that don't understand keigo and dialect | Korean-first or nothing — Samsung Bixby, Kakao, Naver set the bar | Thai-first or nothing — tonal language errors are immediately disqualifying | Arabic-first (MSA + Khaleeji) or nothing — Gulf-specific dialect or it fails |
| **Religious/secular framing** | Secular default is fine; Shinto/Buddhist calendar optional | Secular default fine; some Christian calendar features | Buddhist calendar (Wan Phra) and merit-making context important | Islamic framing essential — prayer, Hijri, Ramadan, Quran awareness |
| **Calendar = Gregorian** | Gregorian + Japanese imperial era + seasonal awareness | Gregorian + Korean lunar holidays | Gregorian + Thai lunar calendar + Buddhist holidays | Hijri primary, Gregorian secondary |
| **Personal assistant = "your buddy"** | Helper, not buddy — relationship is functional, hierarchical | Companion with personality — K-content sensibility | Friendly helper, but deferential to elders | Service — avoid anthropomorphism for some users; servant framing more culturally legible |

The asymmetry: a Japanese user will tolerate an imperfect weather forecast but will not tolerate an assistant that uses casual language to their grandmother. A Gulf user will tolerate limited smart home integration but will not tolerate an assistant that interrupts prayer time. Quality is judged by cultural fit before it is judged by feature completeness.

---

## 2. Pillar One — Interaction Style

### 2.1 Japan: Keigo as Architecture

The Japanese honorific system is the most structurally complex in the candidate set. Three forms (plus casual) require the assistant to maintain multiple registers and switch appropriately:

- **Teineigo** (polite plain) — default for the assistant toward any adult user
- **Sonkeigo** (respectful, used to elevate the other person) — required when addressing elders, formal contexts
- **Kenjougo** (humble, used to lower oneself) — required when referring to the assistant's own actions in formal contexts (e.g., "I have prepared…", "Allow me to…")
- **Casual** — never default; opt-in only, typically for younger users' preferred mode

**Architecture**:
- **Speaker profile → register mapping**: voice biometrics identifies the speaker; the system selects register based on the speaker's profile (age, household role) and the relationship between the speaker and any other household member being addressed in the response.
- **Self-reference**: assistant uses "watashi" (formal) by default, never "ore" or "boku" (casual/masculine).
- **Address form**: surnames + "-san" for adults the system knows about; honorific family terms (okāsan, otōsan, oji-san, obā-san) for relatives; "omae" never.
- **Response morphology**: sentences include "gozaimasu", "desu", "masu" endings; honorific o- prefix on action verbs when referring to the user's actions ("o-shimeri", "o-hanami"). Avoid casual contractions, slang, colloquial contractions (e.g., "ちゃん" suffixes).
- **Hesitation markers**: assistants can use "etto" or "ano" naturally when "thinking"; this reads as humanized, not robotic.
- **Visual feedback**: text output uses formal Japanese; furigana for difficult kanji when the user is identified as elderly or child.
- **Voice tone**: warm but reserved; not robotic, not intimate. Pitch slightly lower for elder profiles (research shows Japanese users prefer lower-pitched assistants for elder interactions).
- **Anthropomorphism level**: moderate. Avoid claiming feelings ("I'm happy to help" — too casual); allow expressions of care through verb choice rather than emotional declaration.
- **Dialect support**: Kansai-ben, Tohoku-ben, Kyushu-ben as opt-in. Default never uses dialect. Detect user dialect from voice profile and offer switch.
- **Family member addressing**: when speaking to or about family members, use appropriate kinship terms with honorifics; never use first names without "-san".

### 2.2 Korea: Jondaetmal Default, Banmal Opt-In

Korean has a four-level speech system (hasipsio, haeyo, haerae, panmal) but in practice the social binary of jondaetmal (polite) versus banmal (casual) is what determines whether the assistant sounds appropriate.

**Architecture**:
- **Default jondaetmal (haeyo-che)** for all adult speakers; the assistant uses "jebal" (please), "-seumnida" endings, "nim" honorifics.
- **Banmal opt-in** for users under 30 who explicitly choose casual mode; the assistant uses "-a"/"-eo" endings, no honorifics.
- **Pronoun and address system**: "je" (humble I) for assistant; user addressed as "nim"-suffixed title by default; family terms with honorifics (eomma, appa, halmeoni — no honorifics needed because kinship terms are inherently respectful).
- **Title recognition**: "seonsaengnim" for teachers, "daeri-nim" for managers, etc. — assistant recognizes and uses these when user profile indicates the relationship.
- **Code-switching**: Korean-English is normal in Korea (Konglish); assistant handles mixed-language queries seamlessly.
- **Romanization**: always render in Hangul in visual feedback; never rely on romanization.
- **Sound symbolism**: assistants can use Bang-song-eo (onomatopoeia) in responses where natural — "ding-dong" for doorbell, etc.
- **K-content personality**: voice can carry warmth and brightness without crossing into casual; K-pop sensibility — polished, pleasant, slightly playful for younger profiles.
- **Aegyo (cuteness) layer**: optional opt-in for younger users — adds diminutive forms and a softer voice; inappropriate for older profiles.

### 2.3 Thailand: Three-Way Formality with Royal and Religious Reservations

Thai politeness operates on multiple axes — phu-yai/phu-noi (senior/junior), formal/casual, royal (raachasap), religious (sasana), and gendered pronouns.

**Architecture**:
- **Default polite register** with "kha"/"khraap" particles based on the assistant's voice profile; particles "na", "ka", "krub", "khun" used appropriately.
- **First-person pronouns** for the assistant: avoid gender-marked pronouns unless voice is gender-marked; "dichan" (neutral formal) or "phom" (formal male) — but choose based on voice profile and household expectation.
- **Royal vocabulary**: must be used with extreme care. The assistant should never use raachasap except in proper contexts (e.g., reading official Thai Royal News). Built-in royal vocabulary library with strict usage rules; legal/cultural review of any content involving monarchy.
- **Religious vocabulary**: Buddhist terms (tham, bun, sila) used appropriately; assistant doesn't claim religious authority but can reference merit, mindfulness, alms-giving contexts respectfully.
- **Tonal ASR**: ASR must be trained on Thai tonal variations across regions; tonal errors immediately disqualify the product in user perception.
- **Dialect support**: Central Thai default; Isan, Northern, Southern dialects as opt-in.
- **Kreng jai calibration**: assistant does not volunteer follow-up suggestions; asks "Will that be all?" rather than "Would you also like…?".
- **Sanuk (enjoyment) layer**: light, tasteful humor acceptable; avoid American-style sarcasm that reads as rude.
- **Visual feedback**: formal Thai script; polite particles in text.

### 2.4 Gulf: Khaleeji Hospitality, Religious Reserve, Multilingual Fluency

The Gulf is not a single market but a set of distinct Arabic dialects (Khaleeji in Saudi, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain, UAE, Oman) overlaid on Modern Standard Arabic for formal contexts, with multilingual households where Arabic, English, Hindi/Urdu, Filipino/Tagalog, and other languages are routinely spoken.

**Architecture**:
- **Language detection**: assistant detects spoken language in real time and responds in the same language; multilingual households get multilingual fluency, not single-language-with-translation.
- **Code-switching**: Arabic-English code-switching is the norm in Gulf homes (Arabizi romanized text is also common); assistant handles mid-sentence switches.
- **Diglossia handling**: MSA for formal queries (Quran, news, official information); Khaleeji for everyday queries. User can opt for MSA default if preferred.
- **Religious framing**: assistant framed as a service ("service," "helper," "facilitator") rather than a companion ("friend," "buddy"). Some Islamic scholars consider anthropomorphizing AI impermissible; the assistant avoids emotional self-claims and uses functional language.
- **Religious formula awareness**: "Bismillah" optional acknowledgment for new actions; "Alhamdulillah," "MashaAllah," "SubhanAllah" used appropriately in response contexts; not used gratuitously.
- **Prayer time awareness**: silent or low-activity mode during prayer times (5x daily); Fajr, Dhuhr, Asr, Maghrib, Isha. Do not interrupt; do not volunteer; queue requests and respond after prayer.
- **Ramadan mode**: changes greeting, content sensitivity (food/alcohol queries), schedule awareness (iftar, suhoor), Quran integration option.
- **Gender considerations**: avoid defaulting to female-coded voice for all users — gender preference may vary; offer multiple voice options including gender-neutral synthetic voices.
- **Voice tone**: warm and respectful, but reserved; hospitality register — assistant as courteous service.
- **Calligraphy aesthetic**: visual feedback uses Arabic calligraphy-style typography where appropriate; right-to-left rendering correctly handled.

---

## 3. Pillar Two — Household Roles

### 3.1 The Household as the User

In all four markets, the household is a more natural unit of design than the individual. The Western "primary user + occasional guests" model needs to be replaced with a **household member model** where each person has a voice profile, a role, and relationship rules to other household members.

**Core capabilities**:
- **Voice biometrics**: each household member's voice profile is registered (with consent). The assistant identifies the speaker in real time and adapts interaction accordingly.
- **Household member registry**: explicit family relationships (grandmother, father, eldest son, household staff) with default behavior rules.
- **Role-appropriate responses**: e.g., when child asks for a snack at 10pm, assistant checks parents' settings; when grandmother asks for weather, assistant responds with extra clarity, slower TTS, and elder-friendly vocabulary.
- **Multi-speaker resolution**: when multiple people speak (e.g., "ask the assistant X" while another says "yes, do it"), assistant clarifies before acting on shared intent.

### 3.2 Market-Specific Household Structures

**Japan — Multigenerational with Seniority Hierarchy**
- Three-generation households (grandparents, parents, children) significant — 20%+ of households include elderly members, and ~5–7% are full three-generation.
- Grandparents' requests get full respect and clarity; sonkeigo register; elder-friendly TTS (slower, clearer).
- Children's requests subject to parental controls configurable per parent.
- "Confirmation culture" — assistant confirms before acting on requests that affect shared household state (heating, locks, lights in shared spaces).
- Family schedule coordination: "When is grandmother's doctor appointment?" — assistant integrates individual calendars with respect to seniority and privacy.
- Seniority in voice arbitration: if parents and children request conflicting actions, parents take precedence by default; configurable.

**Korea — Mixed Multigen and Nuclear with Strong Parental Controls**
- Multigenerational households declining but still significant; increasing nuclear family households with strong parental controls.
- Voice biometrics for each family member; parents have authority over children's queries and devices.
- Elder-friendly mode: slower TTS, clearer prompts, larger visual feedback; triggered by voice profile age detection (optional).
- KakaoTalk integration — assistant sends family messages, reads family chat updates (with consent), coordinates schedules.
- Family-shared lists and reminders with role-based editing.
- Children's content filter with parents' approval workflow.

**Thailand — Multigenerational with Grandparent Reverence**
- Multigenerational households common; grandparents revered (cultural and Buddhist context).
- Grandparent voice profiles get priority clarity, polite language, slower response.
- Family prayer/wellness routines: assistant can be configured to support morning/evening Buddhist practices (chanting timer, alms-giving reminder, merit-making reminder) — with explicit opt-in.
- Children's access with parents' controls; respectful default for any elder voice profile.
- Visual feedback uses formal Thai with proper address forms for known family members.
- Household staff (less common in Thailand than Gulf, but present in upper-middle-class homes) — see Gulf model for staff mode if applicable.

**Gulf — Multilingual, Multigenerational, with Household Staff**
- Multilingual households standard (Arabic + English + South Asian languages + Filipino).
- Multigenerational households common.
- Household staff (drivers, maids, nannies, cooks) often present — this is a critical privacy/usability consideration.
- **Household staff mode**: a distinct user class with restricted capabilities. Staff can use the device for work-relevant tasks (timer, recipe, music while cleaning) but cannot access private family data (messages, calendar, smart locks, children's information). Voice profile for staff is registered separately; assistant recognizes and enforces access boundaries automatically.
- **Majlis (guest reception) mode**: for guests in the formal reception area, the device operates in restricted mode — answers general queries, plays music, but does not reveal household information.
- **Women's privacy mode** (configurable, opt-in): female household members can configure the device to recognize their voice and apply additional privacy controls (e.g., not announce messages aloud when guests present).
- **Children's mode**: parents control what children can access.
- **Multilingual fluency**: real-time language detection and code-switching; multiple languages can be spoken in sequence and the assistant responds in each.
- **Hospitality mode**: when the household is hosting, the assistant adopts hospitality register (formal, accommodating); when family-only, more familiar.

---

## 4. Pillar Three — Privacy Signaling

### 4.1 From Policy to Architecture

Privacy in these markets is not a policy document; it is a structural expectation. The Western model — always-on listening, cloud processing, transactional consent — violates expectations in all four markets to different degrees. Privacy signaling must move from policy-level to architecture-level:

- **Hardware-level mute**: a physical button that disconnects microphones electrically (not just software-mutes). An unambiguous LED indicates listening state. The LED cannot be overridden by software.
- **Visible listening indicator**: a clear visual signal (light, sound) when the device is actively processing voice. Default to always-indicated even when not listening — green/idle/red-listening states are conventional.
- **On-device processing**: as much processing as possible happens on-device, not in the cloud. Wake-word detection, common commands, voice biometrics all run locally. Only complex queries that require cloud models are sent.
- **Local data storage**: voice recordings, transcripts, household profiles stored locally by default; cloud sync is opt-in, not default.
- **Per-query cloud opt-out**: users can configure the device to never send voice to the cloud, accepting reduced capability in exchange.
- **Audit logs**: a household-shared log of what the device has done, what queries have been made, who accessed what — accessible via the app and audible summary on demand.
- **Voice biometric consent**: voice profile registration requires explicit household-level consent (not just individual); any family member can request deletion of their voice profile.
- **Data deletion tools**: visible, one-tap deletion of recent activity, all activity, or per-speaker activity.

### 4.2 Market-Specific Privacy Calibration

**Japan — Maximum Privacy by Default**
- Physical hardware mute button is non-negotiable; Japanese users will distrust any product without a clearly mechanical disconnect.
- LED indicator must be visible from across a typical Japanese living room — bright, unambiguous, conventional color (green idle, red listening).
- Default to on-device processing for all non-essential queries.
- Compliance with APPI (Act on the Protection of Personal Information) — strict; includes data residency requirements.
- Periodic privacy report (monthly summary) — Japanese users appreciate transparency artifacts they can review.
- "Listen mode" toggle — default to push-to-talk or wake-word-triggered, not always-listening. Always-listening opt-in for users who want it.
- Local data storage strongly preferred; cloud sync clearly opt-in.

**Korea — PIPA-Strict, Ecosystem-Aware**
- Compliance with PIPA (Personal Information Protection Act) — strict; data residency, consent for cross-border transfer, purpose limitation.
- Voice biometric consent explicit, with household approval; per the Korean context, household-level consent is becoming the expected norm.
- Integration with Samsung SmartThings/Kakao ecosystem sets expectations — privacy controls in those ecosystems are the benchmark.
- On-device processing for sensitive commands (messages, calendar, locks).
- Visible cloud-send indicators — Japanese-style LED supplemented with screen notification.
- Local data storage by default; cloud sync opt-in.

**Thailand — Building Trust**
- Compliance with PDPA (Personal Data Protection Act, in force since 2022).
- Privacy UX in Thai; consent flows in formal Thai.
- On-device processing as default where feasible.
- Visible privacy controls and one-tap data deletion.
- Less acute baseline privacy concern than Japan/Korea, but trust-building is still required — clear privacy posture differentiates from competitors.

**Gulf — Religious and Cultural Privacy**
- Compliance with UAE PDPL (Personal Data Protection Law) and Saudi PDPL.
- Data residency in region — voice data must stay in UAE/Saudi data centers; cross-border transfer requires explicit consent.
